title: The Term "Open Source" Is Younger Than Linux (1998)
explainer: The phrase "open source" did not exist until February 1998, when a group of programmers and advocates met in Palo Alto after Netscape announced it would release the source code of its Navigator browser; Christine Peterson is generally credited with proposing the term as friendlier to businesses than "free software." Within months the Open Source Initiative (OSI) was founded to formally define what licenses qualify as open source, which is why real projects carry specific license files (MIT, GPL, Apache) rather than just being posted publicly. Knowing the label itself is a late-1990s branding and licensing effort, layered onto decades of pre-existing shared-source culture, helps explain why contribution logistics today revolve so heavily around license compliance and CLAs.
